executive_summary: March 2026 paints a picture of a market where institutional and individual investors are living in different emotional neighborhoods. Institutional investors are deeply split — only half expect prices to rise over the next year, yet every single one surveyed believes a 3% daily drop would bounce back within two days. Individual investors, meanwhile, have turned notably gloomier on the 12-month outlook, with just a third expecting gains. Crash anxiety remains elevated for both groups, and most respondents continue to see the market as overvalued — though that judgment depends on whether you think 'overvaluation' is even a meaningful concept.

key_findings.headline: Individual Optimism Fades Fast
key_findings.interpretation: Only a third of individual investors expect higher prices in a year, down sharply from nearly 58% in February. Institutional confidence held flat at 50% — a coin-flip outlook that may reflect genuine uncertainty rather than conviction in either direction.

key_findings.headline: Crash Fears Linger Unevenly
key_findings.interpretation: Individual crash confidence dropped back to 20%, meaning four out of five wealthy individuals think a crash is at least plausible in the next six months. Institutional confidence slipped modestly from 54% to 50%, suggesting professionals are roughly split on whether to worry.

key_findings.headline: Pros and Public Diverge Sharply
key_findings.interpretation: Every institutional respondent in March said a 3% drop would fully recover within two days — a striking unanimity that could reflect deep faith in market resilience or simply a small sample speaking with one voice. Individual investors moved in the opposite direction, falling from 81% to 40%.

key_findings.headline: Overvaluation Concerns Persist
key_findings.interpretation: Most individual investors still see the market as too expensive, while institutional opinion is evenly split. It's worth noting that investors who believe markets are efficient would consider the 'right price' question essentially unanswerable — the current price is the correct one by definition.

detailed_analysis:
The March data is defined by a dramatic split in the Buy-on-Dips index. Institutional investors hit 100% — unanimous confidence that a sharp one-day drop would snap back quickly. Individual investors went the other way, falling from 81% to 40%. That's one of the widest gaps we've seen between the two groups on any single index. It could reflect professionals' experience with recent recoveries, or it could be an artifact of a small survey sample catching a particular mood.

On the 12-month outlook, individual investors have grown considerably more pessimistic over the quarter — sliding from 67% in January to just 33% in March. Institutional investors, by contrast, dropped from 82% in January to 50% in February and stayed there. One reading of this: everyday investors may be reacting to headlines or personal portfolio pain, while professionals have settled into a wait-and-see posture.

Crash anxiety tells a nuanced story. Only 20% of individuals feel confident a crash won't happen — the same low reading as January, suggesting their baseline worry never really lifted even when February showed a modest improvement. Institutional investors are more evenly divided at 50%, down slightly from February's 54%. Neither group is sounding an all-clear.

Valuation confidence remains subdued across the board. Individual investors at 40% and institutions at 50% both suggest that a meaningful share of respondents view current prices as stretched. That said, this index always deserves an asterisk: some sophisticated investors reject the premise entirely, viewing the market price as inherently correct. For them, this question is a bit like asking whether today's weather is overvalued.
methodology: These indices come from the Yale/Shiller U.S. Stock Market Confidence Surveys, which have tracked investor sentiment since 1989. Each month, roughly 100 wealthy individual investors and 100 institutional investment managers answer the same standardized questions. The consistency of those questions over 35+ years is what makes the data meaningful — you can actually compare investor psychology across very different market environments. The four indices each measure something distinct: • 1-Year Confidence: The share who expect prices to be higher in 12 months. • Crash Confidence: The share who believe a crash in the next 6 months is very unlikely (under 10% probability). A low reading means most people think a crash is plausible. • Buy-on-Dips Confidence: The share who believe that after a 3% single-day market drop, prices would fully recover within two days. • Valuation Confidence: The share who do not believe the market is overvalued. Surveys were conducted semi-annually before 2001 and have been monthly since July 2001. Respondents rotate over time, but consistent characteristics — high income, investment experience — are maintained across the panel.
